plan.taskTitle: Write a 10-page WWI causes research paper by Friday
plan.analysis: With only three days left, this compresses about 11 hours of work into short daily sessions, with ugly drafting kept separate from polishing and everything substantive finished before Friday.

steps.title: Open the doc and paste in the prompt
steps.description: Create a new doc named 'WWI paper - UGLY DRAFT', paste in the assignment prompt and the Friday deadline, and type 'Rough drafts only' at the top. Done when the doc is saved and open.

steps.title: Gather 5-6 sources
steps.description: Find 5-6 sources on WWI causes: your textbook chapter, plus a few library or Google Scholar items on alliances, militarism, imperialism, nationalism, and the July Crisis. Paste the links or citations into the doc and stop at 6, even if they aren't perfect.

steps.title: Skim sources and jot messy notes
steps.description: Skim the intro, conclusion, and headings of each source and write 3-4 bullet points per source on the causes. Bullet fragments are fine. Stop when every source has notes.

steps.title: Sketch a bullet-point outline
steps.description: Write a one-sentence thesis guess (it can change) and 5-6 section headings, such as the alliance system, militarism and the arms race, imperial rivalries, nationalism in the Balkans, the Franz Ferdinand assassination and July Crisis, and the Schlieffen Plan. Put your notes under each heading. Stop after 30 minutes, even if it feels rough.

steps.title: Ugly draft: intro and first two sections
steps.description: Set a timer and write the intro plus the alliance and militarism sections, about 4 pages. Don't edit or delete anything and leave '[CITE]' placeholders where needed. Stop when the timer ends.

steps.title: Ugly draft: middle sections
steps.description: Draft the imperialism, nationalism and Balkans, and July Crisis sections, about 4 pages, using your bullets as prompts. Bad sentences are fine. Stop when you've covered each heading.

steps.title: Ugly draft: conclusion and gaps
steps.description: Write a rough conclusion that ties the causes together and says which mattered most, then fill any page-count gap with more detail on your weakest section. Done when you have a complete draft of about 10 pages, however messy.

steps.title: Polish pass 1: argument and structure
steps.description: Read the draft top to bottom, fix your thesis in the intro so it matches what you actually argued, and reorder or cut paragraphs that drift. Do not fix typos yet. Stop after one read-through.

steps.title: Polish pass 2: citations and bibliography
steps.description: Replace every '[CITE]' placeholder with a real citation and build your bibliography in the required style. Done when no placeholders remain.

steps.title: Final proofread and submit
steps.description: Read once for typos and formatting, then submit. 'Good enough and on time' is the finish line. Done when the file is uploaded or handed in.

grade.notes: Step 1 is tiny and concrete, but step 2 (30 min) is also scheduled today, and several steps are 30-45 min with multiple actions bundled in (e.g. review + cards), which is still sizable for an overwhelmed student. Ch 5-6 flashcards are made but 7 has none, the schedule is uneven, and reassurance is present but mostly generic.

plan.taskTitle: Study for organic chemistry midterm (chapters 5-9)
plan.analysis: Split the five chapters into one small session per day through Monday, then finish with a practice exam and a quick review, so no single step feels big.

steps.title: Set up your study spot
steps.description: Put your o-chem textbook, notes, and a pen on your desk. Write 'Ch 5, 6, 7, 8, 9' on a sticky note and stick it on the book. That's all, and you're done.

steps.title: Review Chapter 5
steps.description: Read the chapter 5 summary and your notes, and write down the key reactions on one page. Done when you have that one page, nothing more.

steps.title: Review Chapter 6
steps.description: Read the chapter 6 summary and your notes, and write the key mechanisms on one page. This step stands alone, so don't worry about the other chapters.

steps.title: Make flashcards for Ch 5-6
steps.description: Turn your two summary pages into flashcards, with a reaction or mechanism on the front and the answer on the back. Done when every item on those pages has a card.

steps.title: Review Chapter 7
steps.description: Read the chapter 7 summary and your notes, and write the key reactions on one page. Stop when the page is filled.

steps.title: Do end-of-chapter problems for Ch 5-7
steps.description: Do 4-5 end-of-chapter problems from each of chapters 5, 6, and 7. Check the answers and circle the ones you missed.

steps.title: Review Chapter 8
steps.description: Read the chapter 8 summary and your notes, write the key points on one page, and make cards for them. You can stop after this one chapter.

steps.title: Review Chapter 9
steps.description: Read the chapter 9 summary and your notes, write the key points on one page, and make cards for them. After this, every chapter has been covered.

steps.title: Mixed problem set Ch 5-9
steps.description: Do 2-3 end-of-chapter problems from each of chapters 5-9, mixed together. Check the answers and mark the ones you got wrong.

steps.title: Take a practice exam
steps.description: Use your professor's old exam or a mixed set from chapters 5-9. Time yourself, answer without notes, and then grade it.

steps.title: Fix your weak spots
steps.description: Pick the 3 topics you missed most on the practice exam. Reread them and redo those problems until you get them right.

steps.title: Final skim and pack your bag
steps.description: Flip through your flashcards once and read your one-page summaries. Pack your pen, ID, and anything else you need. You've already done the hard work.

grade.notes: Timing is vague ("Today"/"Tonight"/"Tomorrow" with no clock times) and step 8 doesn't say the set must be submitted before the deadline. The plan also doesn't account for the problem count: the starred-easy count is unknown, and steps 5-6 leave gaps for the remaining problems. plan.taskTitle: Finish calc problem set 4 (12 problems)
plan.analysis: With the deadline tomorrow, split the 12 problems into small tonight sessions with breaks, then use a short, gentle review tomorrow morning before turning it in.

steps.title: Just set up your workspace
steps.description: Grab a pencil, paper and your calculator, and open problem set 4 so it's sitting in front of you. That's it for now. Done means everything is on your desk and you don't have to solve anything yet.

steps.title: Just read through all 12 problems
steps.description: Skim the whole set and put a small star next to any problem that looks easy or familiar. No solving, just a peek. Done means you know where the easy wins are.

steps.title: Just do the starred easy problems
steps.description: Work through only the ones you starred, and give yourself permission to skip anything that feels sticky. Done means those problems have written answers, even rough ones.

steps.title: Just take a real break
steps.description: Stand up, get a snack or some water, and step away from the screen for a bit. Done means you're back at your desk feeling a little refreshed.

steps.title: Just tackle the next 4 unsolved problems
steps.description: Pick the next four problems in order and work each one, checking your notes or the textbook examples when you get stuck. Done means each has an attempt written out, even if you are unsure.

steps.title: Just give the leftover problems a first try
steps.description: Look at what's still unsolved and write down the first step for each one, then see how far you get. Mark any that still stump you with a question mark. Done means every problem has at least something on the page.

steps.title: Just look up help for the question-mark problems
steps.description: For each problem you flagged, check your lecture notes, a worked example in the textbook, or message a classmate or your TA. Done means you've tried one source of help for each stuck problem and updated your work.

steps.title: Just do a quick tidy-up and submit
steps.description: Skim each answer for missing signs or units, make sure all 12 are labeled, then turn it in. Done means problem set 4 is submitted and you can relax.

plan.taskTitle: Send 5 software engineering summer internship applications by Oct 15

steps.title: Open a doc and a tracker

steps.title: Dig up your current resume

steps.title: Gather 8 possible listings
steps.description: Just spend a little time on LinkedIn, Handshake, or your school's career page and paste the links to 8 summer SWE internships into your doc. No judging yet, only collecting links.

steps.title: Pick your 5 and note deadlines

steps.title: Gently update your resume
steps.description: Just add your most recent project or class and fix any outdated lines. Save it as a PDF named 'FirstLast_Resume.pdf' and you're done.

steps.title: Write one flexible cover letter template
steps.description: Just write a short 3-paragraph template: who you are, one project you're proud of, why this company. Leave blanks for company name and a specific detail.

steps.title: Submit application #1
steps.description: Just do one application: fill in the form, tailor two sentences in the template, upload the resume, and hit submit. Mark it in your tracker.

steps.title: Submit application #2

steps.title: Submit application #3

steps.title: Submit application #4
steps.description: Just do the next one at an easy pace. Done when it's submitted and logged.

steps.title: Submit application #5
steps.description: Just finish the last one. You can celebrate once it's sent and your tracker shows 5 of 5.

steps.title: Buffer check and tidy-up
steps.description: Just look over your tracker and confirm each application sent a confirmation email. If one slipped or failed, fix it now. If all is well, you're done.

steps.title: Extra time for any stragglers
steps.description: Just use this session for anything unfinished, like a form that errored or a missing recommender. If nothing is left, take the win and rest.

grade.notes: Sequence has flaws: step 2 gathers laundry Thursday but washing isn't started until Saturday, and 'put bedding in next load' conflicts with a made bed with clean sheets Sunday; step 5 returns dishes after trash was set by the door. Boredom adaptation is decent (timers, playlist, photo reward) but only step 2 adds real variety/gamification.

plan.taskTitle: Clean my room by Sunday
plan.analysis: Split the cleanup into short, timeboxed, varied sessions across Thursday to Sunday, starting with a 3-minute trash grab, so no single session feels dull or overwhelming.

steps.title: Trash bag sweep
steps.description: Grab a trash bag and set a 3-minute timer. Collect every obvious piece of trash you can see, then tie the bag and set it by the door. Done when the timer rings.

steps.title: Laundry round-up
steps.description: Set a 20-minute timer and play a favorite playlist. Gather all clothes on the floor, chair and bed into a hamper, and hang or fold clean clothes. Challenge: finish before the third song ends.

steps.title: Clear and wipe the desk
steps.description: Set a 25-minute timer. Take everything off your desk, toss or file the junk, wipe the surface, and put back only what you use daily. Done when the desk surface is clear except for those items.

steps.title: Start the laundry load
steps.description: Carry the hamper to the washer and start a load, then put your bedding in the next load if you can. Done when the machine is running and the hamper is empty.

steps.title: Surfaces and floor-items reset
steps.description: Set a 30-minute timer. Put away stray items on your dresser, shelves and nightstand, and return dishes and cups to the kitchen. Done when no dishes remain and every item has a home.

steps.title: Fresh bed and put away laundry
steps.description: Set a 25-minute timer. Make the bed with clean sheets and fold or hang the finished laundry into your drawers and closet. Done when the bed is made and the hamper is empty.

steps.title: Vacuum and final check
steps.description: Set a 20-minute timer. Vacuum or sweep the floor, wipe the dresser top, and take the trash out. Do a quick walkthrough and snap a photo of the finished room as your reward.

grade.notes: The first step is concrete but bundles three actions (create the deck, add 10 slides, message the group), and the slide-skeleton step is oddly placed after the group is told to claim slides. Timing is slightly off: the 'Today' step is first, but step 5 (framing slides) and step 6 (group check-in) both land on Saturday, so the integration work is bunched up, and the 'Tomorrow' and 'Thursday' labels are redundant since Thursday is tomorrow.

plan.taskTitle: Finish 10-slide Tesla marketing strategy presentation for Business 101 group project
plan.analysis: Start with a tiny setup action, then pace research, drafting, group coordination, and rehearsal across Thursday through Sunday so everything is done before Monday 9am.

steps.title: Create the shared deck and message the group
steps.description: Create a new Google Slides file named 'Business 101 - Tesla Marketing', add 10 blank slides, and paste the link into your group chat with the note 'Deck is here, claim slides by tomorrow.' Done when the link is sent.

steps.title: Set up the slide skeleton and split the work
steps.description: Title the 10 slides: Title, Company Overview, Target Customers, Product, Pricing, Place/Distribution, Promotion (no ads, Elon/social media), Brand and Community, Competitors/SWOT, Conclusion. Put each group member's name on their slides in the speaker notes, or agree on this in the chat.

steps.title: Research your assigned sections
steps.description: Using Tesla's investor relations site, your textbook's marketing chapter, and 2-3 news articles, collect 3-4 facts or figures per assigned slide in the speaker notes. Done when each of your slides has sourced bullet points.

steps.title: Draft your slides
steps.description: Turn your notes into slide content with a clear headline, 3 short bullets maximum, and one chart or image per slide. Done when none of your slides are blank.

steps.title: Draft the framing slides
steps.description: Write the Title, Conclusion, and 4Ps summary slides, and check that the whole deck follows the 4Ps (product, price, place, promotion) structure from class. Done when the story from slide 1 to slide 10 flows.

steps.title: Group check-in and gap fill
steps.description: Hold a 30-minute call or chat to review everyone's slides, flag missing parts, and assign fixes. Then fix your own flagged items. Done when every slide has content from its owner.

steps.title: Unify design and add citations
steps.description: Apply one font, one color scheme, and consistent image sizing across the deck, then add a sources line to each slide or a references slide. Done when the deck looks like one person made it.

steps.title: Rehearse out loud and finalize
steps.description: Run through the whole deck with a timer, practice your own slides and the handoffs, and fix any awkward wording or typos. Done when you can present within the time limit and the final file is saved or exported as PDF.

grade.notes: Step 5 has a mismatch (30-min timer but 45 min estimate), and the total of 3h18 doesn't match the step sum (~178 min). The first step also requires finding the prompt and book, and the plan has only light variety beyond timers and challenges.

plan.taskTitle: Read Gatsby chapters 3-4 and write a 1-page response
plan.analysis: With the deadline tomorrow, I compressed the work into tonight (reading in timed chunks with a small hook each) and a short writing session Thursday morning, leaving time for a final check.

steps.title: Set up your doc and book
steps.description: Open a new doc named 'Gatsby Ch 3-4 Response', paste in the assignment prompt, and put your copy of the book open to Chapter 3 next to you. Done when both are open and ready.

steps.title: Read Chapter 3, part one
steps.description: Set a 25-minute timer and read the first half of Chapter 3 (Gatsby's party). Challenge: put a sticky note or a doc line on every spot where something feels off or surprising about Gatsby.

steps.title: Finish Chapter 3
steps.description: Set a 25-minute timer and read the second half of Chapter 3, including the Jordan Baker conversation. Done when you reach the end and have jotted 2 quick notes in your doc.

steps.title: Stand-up break and one-line recap
steps.description: Take a 10-minute break away from screens, then type one sentence in your doc summarizing what Chapter 3 revealed about Gatsby. Done when the sentence is written.

steps.title: Read Chapter 4
steps.description: Set a 30-minute timer and read Chapter 4 (the drive into the city, Wolfsheim, Jordan's story about Daisy). Challenge: list every claim Gatsby makes about himself and mark which ones seem believable.

steps.title: Pick a quote and a thesis sentence
steps.description: Scan your notes and pick one quote from Chapters 3-4 that stands out, then write one sentence saying what it shows about Gatsby, truth, or the American Dream. Done when quote and sentence are in your doc.

steps.title: Draft the response
steps.description: Set a 30-minute timer and write about 400-500 words around your quote: claim, evidence from both chapters, and why it matters. Do not edit while you write, just get to a full page.

steps.title: Edit and submit
steps.description: Read the response aloud, fix awkward lines, trim or extend to one page, check the format, and submit or save it for class. Done when it is turned in.

grade.notes: Step count and sizing suit the task, but the long gaps (Oct to Jan) with no reminders risk the avoider forgetting, and the 'Taxes 2026' folder is fine but the plan doesn't flag that forms can't be entered before late January. plan.taskTitle: File my taxes by April 15
plan.analysis: Spread a gentle, low-pressure plan across the months, starting with a tiny folder setup, gathering documents as they arrive in January, then filing a couple of weeks before April 15.

steps.title: Make a 'Taxes 2026' folder
steps.description: Just create one folder on your computer (or grab a physical envelope) and label it 'Taxes 2026'. Done means the folder exists, even if it's empty.

steps.title: Toss in anything tax-related you already have
steps.description: Just drop in whatever you can find easily, like a past tax return, last year's login info, or a pay stub. No sorting needed, and it's fine if it's only one thing.

steps.title: Jot down your income sources and who might send forms
steps.description: Just write a short list of every job, side gig, scholarship, or bank account that paid you or earned interest this year. Done means you have a list, even if it's rough.

steps.title: Check if someone can claim you as a dependent
steps.description: Just ask a parent or guardian (or look it up) whether they'll claim you. It's a quick yes/no that shapes how you file, and a short text is enough.

steps.title: Collect your tax forms as they arrive
steps.description: Just save any W-2, 1098-T, or 1099 that arrives into your folder, and check your email and student portals for digital copies. Done means every form on your list from step 3 is in the folder or you've noted which are still missing.

steps.title: Pick a filing method
steps.description: Just choose how you'll file: IRS Free File, your school's free tax help (VITA), or a tax app. Write down the choice and create the account if needed.

steps.title: Enter your income forms
steps.description: Just type in your W-2 and any 1099 numbers into the software, one form at a time. Stop when all income is entered, and save your progress.

steps.title: Add education credits and deductions
steps.description: Just enter your 1098-T and answer the student credit questions, like the American Opportunity Credit. Done means the software shows your credits or says you don't qualify.

steps.title: Fill in bank info and personal details
steps.description: Just enter your address, Social Security number, and bank routing and account numbers for any refund. Done means every required field is filled in.

steps.title: Do a calm review of your return
steps.description: Just read through the summary page and check names, numbers, and bank details against your forms. Fix anything that looks off, and ask a friend or VITA volunteer if something is confusing.

steps.title: Hit submit and save your confirmation
steps.description: Just e-file the return and save the confirmation email and a PDF copy in your 'Taxes 2026' folder. Done means you have proof it was accepted, and you can relax.

The sequence also has problems: step 10 cuts to length on Oct 11 before the reader feedback applied on Oct 12, and step 8 follows step 7 on the same day, which undercuts the 'walk away' idea. plan.taskTitle: Write my med school personal statement
plan.analysis: Start with a tiny physical setup step, then separate ugly drafting from polishing, spreading about 12 hours of work evenly across the two weeks with a day of buffer before the deadline.

steps.title: Create the doc and paste in the prompt
steps.description: Open a new doc named 'Med School Personal Statement – UGLY DRAFT', paste in the application's prompt and character/word limit, and type 'Rough drafts are the goal' at the top. Done when the doc is saved and open.

steps.title: Dump your moments in bullet points
steps.description: Set a 30-minute timer and bullet-list every experience that pulled you toward medicine: clinical hours, volunteering, research, a personal story, a moment you doubted yourself. Messy fragments are fine; stop when the timer ends, even if the list feels incomplete.

steps.title: Pick your 2-3 anchor stories and jot why
steps.description: Circle the 2-3 bullets that feel most alive and write 3-5 messy bullets under each on what happened, what you learned, and what it taught you about being a doctor. Done when you have circled stories with notes; no perfect choice needed, you can swap later.

steps.title: Sketch a 5-line skeleton
steps.description: Write one sentence each for: opening scene, anchor story 1, anchor story 2, what you have learned, why medicine. Bad sentences are fine; stop after five lines.

steps.title: Write the ugly first half
steps.description: Using your skeleton, write the opening and first anchor story without editing or deleting anything. Stop after 45 minutes or when you reach the midpoint, even mid-sentence.

steps.title: Write the ugly second half
steps.description: Write the second anchor story, the reflection, and the 'why medicine' ending, with no backspacing or rewording. Done when you have a complete draft start to finish, however rough, in 45 minutes.

steps.title: Walk away, then read it once aloud
steps.description: After a night off, read the draft aloud once and only mark spots with highlights: unclear, boring, or too long. Do not fix anything yet; stop after one pass.

steps.title: Structural rewrite pass
steps.description: Fix only the highlighted big problems: reorder paragraphs, cut anything that is a list of achievements rather than a story, and add missing reflection. Skip word-level polishing; stop at 60 minutes.

steps.title: Send to one trusted reader
steps.description: Email the draft to one advisor, mentor, or pre-med office reader and ask just two questions: 'Does this sound like me?' and 'What is unclear?' Done when it is sent; set a reply-by date of Oct 12.

steps.title: Cut to the length limit
steps.description: Check the word or character count and trim to the limit by removing the weakest sentences first, not by agonizing over wording. Stop when you are under the limit.

steps.title: Apply feedback in one pass
steps.description: Go through your reader's comments and accept only changes that fix confusion or make it sound more like you. Done after one pass of 45 minutes, even if a few comments remain unused.

steps.title: Final line-edit polish
steps.description: Read it aloud once, fixing typos, awkward phrases, and repeated words, and check the length limit again. This is the only polish session; stop at 45 minutes and call it good enough.

steps.title: Paste into the application and submit
steps.description: Copy the final text into the application portal, check formatting and the preview, and save or submit. Done when it is in the system with no more edits.

grade.notes: Time estimates are inflated for a 4-5 sentence email (20 min to draft and 20 min to read and send), and every step just says 'Today' with no concrete times, which matters for a same-day deadline. The first step is good but still requires finding the email, which an avoider might dodge.

plan.taskTitle: Reply to your professor's extension email
plan.analysis: This is a short one-sitting task, so we'll make it tiny: open the email, jot a few facts, write a short draft, and send it today.

steps.title: Just open the email and a blank reply
steps.description: Find your professor's email and click Reply, then leave the reply empty. Done means the blank reply window is open, nothing more.

steps.title: Jot down three quick facts
steps.description: In the reply window or a sticky note, just type three bullets: which assignment, the date it's due now, and the new date you'd like. Done means three rough bullets, no polish needed.

steps.title: Write a short, rough draft
steps.description: Just turn your bullets into 4-5 sentences: a greeting, a brief honest reason, your requested new date, and a thank-you. Done means there are words in the body, even if they're clunky.

steps.title: Read it once and send it
steps.description: Just read it aloud once, fix any typos, check the professor's name and the subject line, and press Send. Done means it's out of your outbox and you can breathe.

grade.notes: Strong, specific plan with a tiny first step, but 14 steps is a lot for an overwhelmed student, and the Sunday, Monday, Tuesday and Oct 7 days are doubled up. Step 12 asks for a lot in one sitting, and 'Friday', 'Oct 7' and 'Oct 8' are inconsistent date formats; case practice also begins only on Tuesday, leaving little buffer.

plan.taskTitle: Get ready for the Deloitte behavioral + case interview
plan.analysis: We'll spread about 7 hours of small, standalone sessions across the 8 days before the interview, covering behavioral stories first and case practice second, with a light review on the day.

steps.title: Open a prep doc and paste in the job posting
steps.description: Create a new doc named 'Deloitte interview prep' and paste in the job posting. That's it, you're done, and this step stands on its own.

steps.title: Highlight 5 skills in the posting
steps.description: Read the posting once and bold five skills or phrases it repeats, such as teamwork, analytics or client focus. Done when you have a five-item list at the top of your doc.

steps.title: List 5 past experiences by headline only
steps.description: Write one line each for five moments from class projects, jobs or clubs, like 'led group project' or 'fixed a conflict'. No details yet, just the headlines.

steps.title: Write STAR notes for 2 stories
steps.description: Pick the first two headlines and jot Situation, Task, Action and Result in bullets for each. Rough notes are fine, so stop when both have all four parts.

steps.title: Write STAR notes for the other 3 stories
steps.description: Do the same quick bullets for your remaining three headlines. Done when all five stories have a Result line, ideally with a number.

steps.title: Skim Deloitte's basics
steps.description: Read Deloitte's About page and its four main service lines (Audit & Assurance, Consulting, Risk & Financial Advisory, Tax). Write 5 bullet facts, including which one your role sits in.

steps.title: Draft two short answers
steps.description: Write 4-5 sentences each for 'Tell me about yourself' and 'Why Deloitte?'. Use your skills list and your bullet facts, and don't aim for perfect.

steps.title: Learn one case framework
steps.description: Search for a beginner guide to profitability cases and write the framework (revenue, costs, drivers) on one page. Done when you can explain it in your own words.

steps.title: Do a short mental math warm-up
steps.description: Do 15-20 practice problems on percentages, growth rates and breakeven with a timer. Stop at 20 minutes even if it feels rough.

steps.title: Practice case #1 out loud
steps.description: Find a free practice case, such as a profitability case, and talk through it aloud with a timer. Afterwards, write down one thing to improve.

steps.title: Practice case #2 out loud
steps.description: Do a second case, ideally a market-entry one, and apply the improvement you noted. Done when you've given a clear recommendation in one or two sentences.

steps.title: Run a mock behavioral round
steps.description: Say your intro, your 'Why Deloitte' answer and three STAR stories out loud, recording on your phone if you like. Note one thing to tighten and fix it.

steps.title: Prep questions and logistics
steps.description: Write 3 questions to ask your interviewers. Then lay out your outfit and confirm the time, location or link, and whom to ask for.

steps.title: Do a final light review
steps.description: Skim your five STAR headlines and your case framework once. Then stop and go in, because you've already done the work.

grade.notes: Step 1 is a good tiny start, though it bundles a few small actions (naming the doc, pasting requirements and data, typing headings). Today's 50 minutes is light with two days left, and Friday is crowded before the 5pm deadline.

plan.taskTitle: Finish and submit Bio 201 enzyme kinetics lab report
plan.analysis: With two days left, the plan starts with a tiny setup action, then spreads data work and writing across Wednesday to Friday morning, leaving time to proofread and submit before 5pm.

steps.title: Set up your report document
steps.description: Create a new doc named 'Bio 201 Enzyme Kinetics Lab Report' and paste in the lab handout's report requirements and your raw data file or lab notebook photos. Done when the doc is open with the headings Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, References typed in.

steps.title: Process your kinetics data
steps.description: Enter your absorbance or rate readings into a spreadsheet and calculate initial reaction velocities for each substrate concentration. Done when you have a clean table of substrate concentration vs. velocity.

steps.title: Make the Michaelis-Menten plot and Lineweaver-Burk plot
steps.description: Graph velocity vs. substrate concentration and the double-reciprocal plot, then estimate Vmax and Km from them. Done when both graphs have labeled axes, units, and captions, and are pasted into the Results section.

steps.title: Write Methods and Results
steps.description: Describe the enzyme, substrate, buffer, and assay procedure in past tense, then write the Results paragraphs that reference your table and figures with the Vmax and Km values. Done when both sections are drafted, even if rough.

steps.title: Write the Introduction and Discussion
steps.description: Write the Introduction covering enzyme kinetics and your hypothesis, then a Discussion interpreting Km and Vmax, comparing to expected values, and naming two sources of error. Done when both sections have full rough drafts.

steps.title: Add the Abstract and References
steps.description: Write a 150-200 word abstract summarizing purpose, methods, key results, and conclusion, then list your textbook and lab manual citations in the required format. Done when the abstract and reference list are complete.

steps.title: Proofread, check the rubric, and submit
steps.description: Read the report aloud once, check figures are numbered and referenced, compare against the handout's rubric, then upload it. Done when you have a submission confirmation before 5pm.

plan.taskTitle: Plan a surprise birthday party for ~15 people
plan.analysis: Work backward from Oct 24 in short, varied, timeboxed sessions, locking in the date and venue first, then invites, food, decor and a surprise cover story, with finishing touches done a day early.

steps.title: Create the party note and start a guest list
steps.description: Open a new note or doc called 'Surprise Party for [Friend]' and type 'Party: Oct 24, ~15 people' at the top. Then paste in 5 names you already know will come, no decisions needed beyond that.

steps.title: Text the co-conspirator and pick a date and time
steps.description: Set a 15-minute timer. Message one close friend of the birthday person to ask for help, then lock in a start time on Oct 24 and note any dietary restrictions they know of. Done when you have a confirmed time and an ally.

steps.title: Finish the guest list of 15
steps.description: Set a 20-minute timer and race to get the list to about 15 names with phone numbers or handles. Ask your ally to fill in gaps, and done means a complete list in your note.

steps.title: Set a budget and venue shortlist
steps.description: Spend 30 minutes deciding a total budget and listing 3 venue options (your place, a friend's place, a rented room or restaurant back room). Done when each option has a price and capacity noted.

steps.title: Call or message venues and book one
steps.description: Set a 30-minute timer and contact your top 3 venues, then book the first one that fits 15 people on Oct 24. Done when you have a written confirmation or a deposit receipt.

steps.title: Write the cover story and send invites
steps.description: Spend 25 minutes drafting a short invite with date, time, address, 'SURPRISE, don't tell' and an arrive-by time 30 minutes early. Send it to the whole list, and agree a cover story with your ally to get the guest of honor there.

steps.title: Plan the menu and drinks
steps.description: Set a 30-minute timer to build a menu with a main, two sides, snacks, drinks and a vegetarian option, using the dietary notes you gathered. Done when you have a shopping or ordering list with quantities for 15.

steps.title: Order the cake and any catering
steps.description: Spend 30 minutes calling or ordering online for the cake (pick their favorite flavor) and any food that needs advance notice. Done when pickup or delivery times are confirmed and in your note.

steps.title: Chase RSVPs
steps.description: Spend 20 minutes messaging anyone who hasn't replied, then update the headcount in your note. Done when you have a final count, plus a reminder to everyone to keep it secret.

steps.title: Plan decor and a playlist, as a game
steps.description: Set a 45-minute timer and challenge yourself: build a 25-song playlist of their favorites, then list decor (banner, balloons, table items) with a shopping list. Done when the playlist is saved and decor is listed.

steps.title: Buy decor and non-perishables
steps.description: Take your list and spend about 60 minutes buying decor, plates, cups, candles and drinks. Done when everything is in a single bag or box by your door.

steps.title: Plan the timeline and assign jobs
steps.description: Spend 30 minutes writing the party-day schedule (setup, guests arrive, surprise moment, cake) and assigning jobs to your ally and 2 other helpers. Send it to them and done means everyone knows their role.

steps.title: Confirm vendors and venue
steps.description: Set a 20-minute timer and re-confirm the venue access time, cake pickup and any catering. Done when all are confirmed and times are in your note.

steps.title: Prep and pack everything
steps.description: Spend 45 minutes pre-wrapping the gift if you have one, printing or finishing signs, charging a speaker and packing the party box. Done when your checklist is fully ticked.

steps.title: Buy fresh food and set up early
steps.description: Spend about 2 hours picking up the fresh food and cake and doing as much setup as the venue allows, with a helper if possible. Done when the room is decorated and food is ready to go.

steps.title: Final setup and send a last reminder
steps.description: Spend about 2 hours at the venue finishing setup, doing a sound check on the playlist and texting guests a 'hide by [time]' reminder. Done when everything is ready before the guest of honor arrives.

grade.notes: The plan sequences some steps poorly and underestimates the work: the 21-hour total is optimistic for a full move, and the final 3-hour move and cleaning steps are crammed into single days. Photos of the rooms (step 15) should come before packing or while rooms are still intact, and cleaning before the move leaves the apartment dirty afterward. plan.taskTitle: Move out of my apartment by end of October
plan.analysis: Moving out is a big multi-week job, so this plan breaks it into many tiny, standalone steps paced evenly through October, with logistics booked early and cleaning saved for the final days.

steps.title: Put 3 empty boxes or bags in your living room
steps.description: Grab any boxes, bags, or laundry baskets and set them where you'll see them. That's it, nothing else needed today.

steps.title: Find your lease and check move-out rules
steps.description: Open your lease or email your landlord and note the move-out date, notice required, and cleaning rules in your phone notes. Done when you have 3 bullet points saved.

steps.title: Send your move-out notice
steps.description: Email or submit your written notice to the landlord if the lease requires it. Done when you hit send and screenshot the confirmation.

steps.title: Write a one-page list of what needs to happen
steps.description: List rough categories: packing, transport, cleaning, utilities, address change, keys. No ordering or deciding needed, just dump them out.

steps.title: Decide how you'll move your stuff and book it
steps.description: Pick one: friend with a car, rental van, or movers. Send the message or booking for a date around Oct 29-30. Done when it's requested or booked.

steps.title: Gather packing supplies
steps.description: Ask friends, a local store, or order boxes, tape, and markers. Done when you have enough for about 10 boxes to start.

steps.title: Pack one shelf or drawer
steps.description: Choose the easiest one, such as books or a desk drawer. Pack it and label the box. One box is a full win.

steps.title: Pack off-season clothes and extra linens
steps.description: Fill boxes with things you won't need before the move. Label them and stack by the wall.

steps.title: Schedule utilities stop and internet cancel
steps.description: Contact providers to end or transfer service for your move-out date. Done when each has a confirmed date written down.

steps.title: Pack decor, books, and desk items
steps.description: Take down wall items and pack books and desk stuff. Stop after 45 minutes even if not finished.

steps.title: Sort a donate or trash pile
steps.description: Set a bag by the door and fill it with things you clearly don't want. Drop it off or put it out when full.

steps.title: Update your address
steps.description: Change your address with the post office, bank, school, and phone carrier. Do just the first two if you're tired; the rest can wait.

steps.title: Pack the kitchen, part 1
steps.description: Pack dishes, appliances, and pantry items you won't use. Keep one plate, one bowl, and one set of utensils out.

steps.title: Pack the bathroom and closet
steps.description: Box up everything except daily essentials and hanging clothes. Label the boxes and you're done.

steps.title: Take dated photos of every room
steps.description: Photograph each room and any damage to protect your deposit. Save them in one album.

steps.title: Pack remaining items and essentials box
steps.description: Pack what's left except bedding and toiletries. Fill a small bag with chargers, keys, and the move-out paperwork.

steps.title: Clean the kitchen and bathroom
steps.description: Wipe counters, scrub the sink, toilet, and shower, and clean out the fridge. Take a break halfway if needed.

steps.title: Clean floors, windows, and surfaces
steps.description: Sweep, vacuum, and mop. Wipe baseboards and doors if you have time.

steps.title: Move your stuff out
steps.description: Load the vehicle or meet the movers and take everything to your new place. Do a last sweep of closets and cabinets.

steps.title: Final walkthrough and return keys
steps.description: Take final photos, turn off lights, lock up, and hand in keys. Done when you have confirmation of the return.

grade.notes: Step 1 is tiny, but it asks for decisions (which app, a sticky note) and Duolingo is never used again, so the daily 'Hola, 15 min' routine isn't backed by later steps. Total time is mislabeled: the steps sum to about 16 hours, not 20, and ~40-minute sessions every 3-4 days is thin for 'getting around'. The 25 steps are repetitive and somewhat heavy, though the variety (role-plays, shows, podcasts, games) suits boredom.

plan.taskTitle: Learn survival Spanish for your Mexico trip
plan.analysis: Build a realistic ~20-hour travel-Spanish routine with short, varied sessions (apps, speaking, listening, role-play) paced evenly from now to Dec 20, with the first step being a tiny physical setup.

steps.title: Set up your Spanish starter kit
steps.description: Download Duolingo (or your chosen app) on your phone, and put a sticky note reading 'Hola, 15 min' on your laptop or bedroom door. Done when the app is open on your home screen and the note is visible.

steps.title: Learn greetings and polite basics
steps.description: Set a 25-minute timer and learn hola, buenos días, por favor, gracias, perdón, con permiso, and cómo está. Done when you can say all seven aloud without looking, and you've recorded yourself saying them once.

steps.title: Make a 40-card survival phrase deck
steps.description: In Anki or Quizlet, create cards for 40 must-know phrases: ordering food, asking 'dónde está...', 'cuánto cuesta', 'no entiendo', 'necesito ayuda'. Done when all 40 cards are in the deck.

steps.title: Numbers 0-100 speed challenge
steps.description: Spend 20 minutes learning numbers, then do a game: say the prices of 10 items around your room in Spanish against the clock. Beat your own time on the second round.

steps.title: Food and restaurant vocabulary
steps.description: Learn 30 menu words (tacos, agua sin gas, la cuenta, sin picante, alergia, etc.) and read a real Mexican restaurant menu online, noting 10 dishes you'd order. Done when you can order a full meal out loud.

steps.title: Flashcard review round 1
steps.description: Set a 20-minute timer and review your phrase deck with the spaced-repetition setting on. Done when you've cleared the day's due cards.

steps.title: Listen to a beginner Spanish podcast episode
steps.description: Play one episode of Coffee Break Spanish or Duolingo Spanish Podcast while walking or doing chores. Jot down 5 words you caught and look them up afterward.

steps.title: Transportation and directions lesson
steps.description: Learn izquierda, derecha, recto, aeropuerto, taxi, autobús, boleto, estación, and 'a qué hora sale'. Then trace a route on Google Maps and narrate directions aloud in Spanish.

steps.title: First role-play: greet and order
steps.description: Find a partner (friend, tutor on iTalki, or an AI chat) and do a 15-minute role-play of arriving at a café and ordering. Done when you've completed the scene, even clumsily.

steps.title: Hotel and lodging lesson
steps.description: Learn reservation, habitación, llave, wifi, 'a qué hora es el desayuno', and 'el aire acondicionado no funciona'. Write a 6-line check-in dialogue and read it aloud twice.

steps.title: Present-tense verb basics
steps.description: Spend 40 minutes on quiero, necesito, puedo, tengo, voy, and estoy with 3 example sentences each about your trip. Done when you've written and spoken 18 sentences.

steps.title: Flashcard review round 2 plus new cards
steps.description: Clear due cards in 20 minutes, then add 20 new cards from your weakest topics (numbers, directions or food). Done when the deck is clear and has 60 cards.

steps.title: Shopping and bargaining lesson
steps.description: Learn 'cuánto cuesta', 'es muy caro', 'me lo llevo', 'puedo pagar con tarjeta', and market phrases. Practice a mock haggling scene aloud with a price list.

steps.title: Watch a Mexican show clip with subtitles
steps.description: Watch 20 minutes of a Spanish-language show with Spanish subtitles. Pause to write down 8 words or phrases you recognized or want to learn.

steps.title: Second role-play: directions and transport
steps.description: Do a 20-minute live or AI role-play of asking for directions to a bus station and buying a ticket. Done when you can complete it without switching to English.

steps.title: Health, emergency and safety phrases
steps.description: Learn 'necesito un médico', farmacia, 'me duele...', 'estoy perdido', 'llame a la policía', and allergy phrases. Save them in a notes app on your phone for offline use.

steps.title: Diagnostic: 15-minute speaking test
steps.description: Record yourself handling five travel scenarios (airport, hotel, restaurant, directions, shop) with no notes. Play it back and mark the three weakest spots.

steps.title: Targeted drills on weak spots
steps.description: Spend two 20-minute rounds drilling the three weak areas from your recording using cards, repetition aloud, and fresh example sentences. Done when you re-record those parts cleanly.

steps.title: Listening practice with native speed
steps.description: Listen to a Mexican Spanish YouTube vlog or news clip for 25 minutes, replaying one short section three times. Write what you understood in a 5-sentence summary.

steps.title: Third role-play: full trip simulation
steps.description: Do a 30-minute session with a partner or tutor simulating airport to hotel to dinner to market. Done when you've covered all four scenes.

steps.title: Mexican Spanish slang and culture quick-hit
steps.description: Spend 25 minutes learning words like ¿qué onda?, mande, ahorita, padre, and tipping and politeness norms. Add 10 new cards.

steps.title: Flashcard review round 3
steps.description: Review the whole deck in a 25-minute timed session, aiming to get 90% right. Re-flag any card you miss for extra review.

steps.title: Build your pocket cheat sheet
steps.description: Make a one-page offline phrase sheet (or phone note) with the top 40 phrases, numbers, and emergency lines. Save a screenshot as a favorite or lock-screen photo.

steps.title: Final speaking challenge
steps.description: Record a 5-minute monologue 'planning my day in Mexico' using only Spanish. Done when you finish without stopping for more than a few seconds.

steps.title: Last light review and confidence check
steps.description: Spend 20 minutes on a final pass through your cheat sheet and weakest cards, then do a quick victory round of the numbers and ordering a meal aloud.

grade.notes: The first step bundles opening the file, finding the function, writing a test that builds a list, and running it, which is more than 5 minutes with several small decisions. The timing is vague, with 'Today' and 'Tonight' used instead of concrete times, so it never shows how the 2 hours fit before 11:59pm.

plan.taskTitle: Fix the node-loss bug in the CS 106 linked list delete function
plan.analysis: Since the deadline is tonight, the plan reproduces the bug with a tiny test, traces pointers on paper, fixes the delete logic, and verifies with edge-case tests before submitting.

steps.title: Open the project and add a failing test
steps.description: Open your assignment file, find the delete function, and add a tiny main/test that builds a list of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, deletes 3, and prints the list. Done when you can run it and see the missing nodes in the output.

steps.title: Trace the delete function on paper
steps.description: Draw the 5 nodes as boxes with arrows and step through your delete code line by line, updating the arrows after each line. Done when you've circled the exact line where the pointer to the rest of the list gets lost.

steps.title: Add print statements around the pointer updates
steps.description: Print the addresses or values of prev, curr, and curr->next before and after each pointer reassignment in delete. Done when the output confirms what your paper trace predicted.

steps.title: Fix the delete logic
steps.description: Rewrite the faulty lines so prev->next is set to curr->next before you free or unlink curr, and never overwrite a pointer before saving it. Done when your 1-5 test prints 1, 2, 4, 5.

steps.title: Test the edge cases
steps.description: Run deletes on the head node, the tail node, the only node in a one-item list, a value that isn't in the list, and an empty list. Done when every case prints the correct list with no crashes or lost nodes.

steps.title: Check for memory leaks and clean up
steps.description: Remove your debug prints, run Valgrind or your language's equivalent checker if available, and confirm deleted nodes are freed exactly once. Done when the code is clean and the checker reports no errors.

steps.title: Submit the assignment
steps.description: Run any provided autograder or sample tests one last time, then upload your files to the course submission page and confirm the receipt. Done when you see the submission confirmation before 11:59pm.

Step 5 (walk away) is filler rather than a real action, and the perfectionist framing could be warmer with more explicit 'done beats perfect' language.

plan.taskTitle: Write a 500-word Psych 101 discussion post on the bystander effect
plan.analysis: Start with a tiny setup action, then draft ugly and rough across a few days, and polish in a separate session with a firm stopping point, finishing a day before Sunday's deadline.

steps.title: Set up your doc and paste in the prompt
steps.description: Open a new doc titled 'Psych 101 bystander effect post', paste in the discussion prompt and the 500-word requirement, and save it. Done when the doc exists with the prompt at the top; do nothing else.

steps.title: Skim your textbook section on the bystander effect
steps.description: Read the bystander effect section in your Psych 101 textbook or lecture notes, and copy down 3-5 messy bullet points, such as Kitty Genovese, Darley and Latané's 1968 study, and diffusion of responsibility. Bullet fragments are fine; stop after 30 minutes even if you feel unfinished.

steps.title: Bullet-point your three main points
steps.description: Under your notes, write three bullets: what the bystander effect is, one study or example that shows it, and one real-life takeaway or opinion. Sloppy shorthand is the goal, and you are done when each bullet has a sentence or two of fragments.

steps.title: Write an ugly first draft
steps.description: Turn your bullets into paragraphs as fast as you can, without editing or deleting anything. Aim for roughly 500 words, but a messy 400 or 600 is fine; stop when you hit the end of your third point or after 45 minutes.

steps.title: Walk away from your draft
steps.description: Close the doc and do something else for a few hours. This is the cooling-off break between drafting and polishing, so do not reread the draft during it.

steps.title: Polish pass: clarity and word count
steps.description: Read your draft once aloud, fix anything confusing, and trim or add to land near 500 words. Fix only things that are clearly wrong or unclear; stop after 40 minutes and call it good enough.

steps.title: Add a discussion hook, proofread, and submit
steps.description: End with one question for classmates, run spell-check, and check the prompt requirements and any citation needs. Then post it, without rereading more than once, for a one-day buffer before Sunday's deadline.

plan.taskTitle: Start going to the gym regularly
plan.analysis: Since there's no deadline, this plan eases you in over about three weeks with tiny, low-pressure steps that build from setting out gear to a steady 3-visits-a-week habit.

steps.title: Put your gym clothes by the door
steps.description: Just grab a shirt, shorts or leggings, socks and shoes and set them in a pile by your door or in a bag. Done when you can see them without opening a drawer.

steps.title: Find out the gym's hours and where it is
steps.description: Just look up your campus rec center or nearby gym and save its opening hours and address in your phone notes. Done when you know the quietest-looking time, with no need to commit to anything.

steps.title: Take a no-workout visit
steps.description: Just walk over, look around, find the lockers and the equipment area, and ask the front desk about sign-up or student access if you need it. You're allowed to leave right after, and that counts as a win.

steps.title: Do a gentle first workout
steps.description: Just do 20 minutes: 10 minutes on a treadmill or bike, then a few easy bodyweight or machine moves. Stop when the timer ends, even if you feel fine.

steps.title: Pick your three gym days
steps.description: Just choose three slots in your calendar for the coming week, like Mon, Wed and Sat, and set a reminder for each. Done when they show up on your phone.

steps.title: Write a tiny starter routine
steps.description: Just jot down 5 easy exercises in your notes app, such as a bike warm-up, leg press, chest press, row machine and plank. Done when it fits on one screen so you never have to decide in the moment.

steps.title: Gym session 1: follow your routine
steps.description: Just show up and do your 5 exercises, 2 sets each, at an easy weight. Done when you've finished the list, even if it's short.

steps.title: Gym session 2
steps.description: Just repeat your routine and add a little, like one more set or a slightly heavier weight on one move. Done when you've logged it in your notes.

steps.title: Gym session 3
steps.description: Just go and do your routine again, then give yourself credit for completing your first full week. Done when you tick it off your calendar.

steps.title: Check in on how it felt
steps.description: Just spend a few minutes noting what you liked, what felt annoying, and one thing to tweak, like a different time or a gym buddy. Done when you have one small change for next week.

steps.title: Week 2 session 1
steps.description: Just go at your best-fitting time and do your routine, adding your one tweak. Done when you've logged it.

steps.title: Week 2 session 2
steps.description: Just show up and do your routine, then try one new machine or exercise at the end for fun. Done when you've written down how it went.

steps.title: Week 2 session 3
steps.description: Just go and finish your routine, then book your next week's three slots before you leave. Done when they're in your calendar.

steps.title: Week 3 session and celebrate
steps.description: Just do one more full session and notice that this is now your third week of going. Done when you've treated yourself to something small, like a smoothie.

steps.title: Keep the habit going
steps.description: Just look at your calendar and confirm your regular gym days for the next month. Done when they're repeating events with reminders.

The plan's sequence has some oddities: Thursday is vague, the 'Tuesday' reference in step 12 is wrong (Nov 10 is a Tuesday, fine), and steps 3, 6, 8 and 11 are unevenly sized. The first step is tiny, but it assumes LawHub and a test date, and the 'admission ticket' and 'test day' reference is an unverified assumption since the deadline is Nov 14. plan.taskTitle: Study for the LSAT in small, steady sessions
plan.analysis: Start with a 5-minute setup, then spread short Logical Reasoning and Reading Comprehension sessions evenly through Nov 13, with a diagnostic first and error-log review after each practice.

steps.title: Set up your LSAT home base
steps.description: Create a free LawHub account at lsac.org, or open it if you have one, and bookmark the page. That's all for today, and nothing else is needed.

steps.title: Do one timed Logical Reasoning section
steps.description: Pick the first Logical Reasoning section in LawHub's free practice, set a 35-minute timer, and finish it. This step stands alone, and your score doesn't matter yet.

steps.title: Start your error log
steps.description: Make a sheet with columns for question number, question type, and why you missed it. Log each wrong answer from that section, and you're done.

steps.title: Drill Flaw questions
steps.description: Read one short lesson on Flaw questions, then do 10 untimed Flaw questions. Add any misses to your error log.

steps.title: Read two Reading Comprehension passages
steps.description: Do 2 passages untimed, summarizing each paragraph in a few words as you go. Stop when both are done.

steps.title: Review those passages
steps.description: Go through every question you missed and write one line on why the right answer wins. Log the misses.

steps.title: Drill Strengthen, Weaken and Assumption questions
steps.description: Do 5 of each type, untimed. Add your misses to the error log with a one-line reason.

steps.title: Do a timed Reading Comprehension section
steps.description: Set a 35-minute timer and do one full RC section. Just finish it, and leave the review for next time.

steps.title: Review your error log patterns
steps.description: Reread your log and circle the 2 question types you miss most. Redo 5 missed questions without looking at the answers.

steps.title: Mixed Logical Reasoning drills
steps.description: Do 15 mixed LR questions, focusing on your two weakest types. Log each miss.

steps.title: Timed LR section plus quick review
steps.description: Do a 35-minute LR section, then spend about 25 minutes reviewing the misses. Compare with your first section, and note any improvement.

steps.title: Do two timed sections back to back
steps.description: Do one LR and one RC section with a 5-minute break between them. Skip the review today, since you'll do it Tuesday.

steps.title: Review the two-section run
steps.description: Go through every miss and update your error log with the reason and the fix. Pick one thing to do differently on test day.

steps.title: Light final review
steps.description: Skim your error log and reread your one test-day tip. Pack your ID and admission ticket, then stop. You're ready.

Some "when" values are vague ("Saturday"), and there is no buffer for advisor feedback or slippage.

plan.taskTitle: Draft and finish thesis Chapter 2 (literature review, ~25 pages)
plan.analysis: Spread about 22 hours of work across the month in a few short sessions per week, with ugly drafting kept separate from polishing and a clear stopping point on every step.

steps.title: Create the Chapter 2 file
steps.description: Open a new doc named 'Thesis Ch2 - UGLY DRAFT', type the heading 'Chapter 2: Literature Review' and save it. Done the moment the file exists; do not write anything else.

steps.title: Dump your sources into one list
steps.description: Paste every paper, book and note you already have for the thesis into the doc as a messy list. Stop at 45 minutes; incomplete and unformatted is fine.

steps.title: Sketch a bullet-point skeleton
steps.description: Write 4-6 rough section headings for the review with 2-3 bullets each naming which sources go where. Bullets are fine, it will be wrong in places, and you stop when the timer ends.

steps.title: Fill gaps in sources, round 1
steps.description: Search for missing key papers for sections 1-2 of your skeleton and add the 5-8 best to your list with one-line notes. Stop at 60 minutes even if you feel there is more.

steps.title: Read and note sources for sections 1-2
steps.description: Skim your sources for the first two sections and write 2-3 sloppy bullets per source: claim, method, how it relates to your question. Stop after 90 minutes, no perfect notes.

steps.title: Ugly draft section 1
steps.description: Write the first section (about 4-5 pages) from your bullets without editing or deleting anything. Placeholders like [CITE?] are allowed; stop at 90 minutes.

steps.title: Ugly draft section 2
steps.description: Write section 2 (about 4-5 pages) the same way, fast and rough. Stop when the time is up even if mid-paragraph.

steps.title: Read and note sources for sections 3-4
steps.description: Skim the sources for sections 3 and 4 and jot rough bullets per source. Stop at 90 minutes.

steps.title: Ugly draft section 3
steps.description: Write section 3 (about 4-5 pages) with no polishing. Leave gaps marked and move on; stop at 90 minutes.

steps.title: Ugly draft section 4
steps.description: Write section 4 (about 4-5 pages) quickly and roughly. Done when the section has a beginning, middle and end, however bad.

steps.title: Ugly draft remaining sections and gap summary
steps.description: Draft any remaining section plus a rough 1-2 page 'gaps in the literature and my contribution' ending. Stop at 2 hours; ugly is the goal.

steps.title: Write the introduction paragraphs
steps.description: Now that you know what the chapter says, write a rough opening of 1-2 pages that previews the sections. Stop at 45 minutes.

steps.title: Fill [CITE?] placeholders
steps.description: Search the doc for every [CITE?] or gap marker and fix each with a source or cut the claim. Stop at 90 minutes; unresolved ones can wait for the polish pass.

steps.title: Structure pass (no sentence editing)
steps.description: Read the whole chapter once and only move, merge or cut paragraphs so the sections flow logically. Do not touch wording; stop at 90 minutes.

steps.title: Polish pass on sections 1-2
steps.description: Now edit sentences and transitions for the first half only. Stop at 90 minutes; good enough is the standard.

steps.title: Polish pass on sections 3-4 and ending
steps.description: Edit the second half and conclusion the same way. Stop at 90 minutes and do not restart earlier sections.

steps.title: Format citations and bibliography
steps.description: Check every in-text citation against your reference list and fix the style. Done when each citation has an entry and vice versa; stop at 90 minutes.

steps.title: Final read-through and typo check
steps.description: Read the chapter once start to finish, fixing only typos and glaring errors. One pass only, stop at 60 minutes.

steps.title: Save, export and send
steps.description: Rename the file 'Thesis Ch2 - v1', export a PDF and send it to your advisor or submission spot. Done when it is sent, even if you still see flaws.

plan.taskTitle: Update resume and LinkedIn before the career fair

steps.title: Rewrite Experience and Projects bullets

steps.title: Get feedback and finalize

plan.taskTitle: Memorize the first 36 elements (H through Kr) for Monday's chem quiz
plan.analysis: Split the 36 elements into three chunks of 12, vary the method each session (flashcards, mnemonics, writing, games), and space out reviews across Thursday to Sunday so everything is locked in before Monday.

steps.title: Set up your flashcard stack
steps.description: Grab 36 index cards (or open a free Quizlet set named 'Elements 1-36') and write the first 5 elements on cards with symbol on one side and name and atomic number on the other. Done when 5 cards sit on your desk or screen.

steps.title: Finish cards and learn elements 1-12 (H to Mg)
steps.description: Make the remaining cards for H through Mg, then set a 20-minute timer and drill them until you get all 12 right twice in a row. Challenge: beat your own time on the last run.

steps.title: Learn elements 13-24 (Al to Cr)
steps.description: Make cards for Al through Cr, then set a 25-minute timer and drill them in shuffled order. Done when you can say all 12 symbols and names without peeking once.

steps.title: Invent silly mnemonics for 1-24
steps.description: Set a 15-minute timer and write the funniest sentence you can for each group of 8 elements (e.g. H, He, Li, Be, B, C, N, O). Done when you have 3 mnemonic sentences saved in your notes app, and you've read them aloud once.

steps.title: Learn elements 25-36 (Mn to Kr)
steps.description: Make cards for Mn through Kr and drill for 25 minutes with a timer, saying each answer aloud. Done when you get all 12 right in a shuffled run.

steps.title: Blank-table writing challenge
steps.description: Set a 15-minute timer and write elements 1-36 in order from memory on blank paper, then check against your textbook periodic table and circle misses. Done when you have a list of your weak elements.

steps.title: Game it: online element quiz
steps.description: Play a timed periodic table game (such as Sporcle or a Quizlet Match round) restricted to elements 1-36 for 20 minutes, focusing on your circled weak ones. Done when you hit a score you're proud of or beat your first attempt.

steps.title: Final mock quiz and weak-spot patch
steps.description: Write all 36 elements again from memory (symbols and atomic numbers) in a 10-minute timed run, then spend 8 minutes re-drilling anything missed. Done when you score 36/36 or are down to 1-2 misses you've re-studied.

grade.notes: Timing is the weak spot: the analysis claims substantive work finishes a day early, but the polish and submit steps are all on Friday, the deadline day, leaving no buffer. Total time is also stated as 4h05 while the steps sum to about 3h25. The perfectionist framing is strong, though the plan could use more explicit 'done beats perfect' language.

plan.taskTitle: Write a cover letter for the Google APM role
plan.analysis: Start with a tiny physical setup, then separate gathering raw material, ugly drafting, and polishing across Wednesday to Friday, finishing substantive work a day early.

steps.title: Set up your cover letter doc
steps.description: Open a new doc named 'Google APM cover letter', paste in the job posting and your resume below it, and save. Done when both are pasted; do not read or think about them yet.

steps.title: Dump raw bullet points
steps.description: Under the job posting, write messy bullets answering: why Google, why product management, and 3 projects or moments from your resume where you led, shipped, or used data. Bullet fragments are fine; stop after 30 minutes or when you have 3 projects listed.

steps.title: Match requirements to your stories
steps.description: Highlight 3 requirements in the posting (e.g. product sense, technical skill, leadership) and write the name of one of your projects next to each. Done when each has a match, even if imperfect; do not rank or agonize.

steps.title: Write the ugly opening and closing
steps.description: Write a rough 3-4 sentence opening (why this role and why Google) and a 2-3 sentence closing. They are allowed to be bad; stop at 25 minutes, and be okay with cliches you will fix later.

steps.title: Write the ugly middle paragraphs
steps.description: Turn your 2-3 matched projects into short paragraphs: what the problem was, what you did, and the result with one number if you have it. Do not edit as you go; stop when each project has a paragraph of any quality.

steps.title: Do a structural pass, no wordsmithing
steps.description: Read the whole draft once and fix only big things: cut anything off-topic, reorder paragraphs, and trim to one page. Done when it fits on one page and flows start to finish; ignore word choice for now.

steps.title: Polish and proofread
steps.description: Fix wording, check for typos, make sure the company and role names are correct, and read it aloud once. Set a 30-minute timer; when it rings, it is finished.

steps.title: Export and submit
steps.description: Save as PDF named with your name and 'Google APM cover letter', upload it to the application, and hit submit. Done when you see the confirmation.

steps.title: Toss everything into the right folder

plan.taskTitle: Build a coffee shop marketing plan with your 3 teammates
plan.analysis: Start by getting the team connected and the assignment in one shared place, then split the plan into sections, work a few sessions per week, and merge and polish before the Oct 20 deadline.

steps.title: Create shared doc and message the team
steps.description: Create a Google Doc called 'Coffee Shop Marketing Plan', paste in the assignment prompt and deadline (Oct 20), and send the link to your 3 teammates in your group chat. Done when the message is sent.

steps.title: Propose a kickoff meeting time
steps.description: In the group chat, suggest two 45-minute meeting slots this week and ask everyone to vote. Done when a time is picked.

steps.title: Kickoff meeting: split sections and roles
steps.description: Meet and list the plan sections: situation analysis, target audience, goals, strategies/channels, budget, timeline, and metrics. Assign each person owner roles, set a mid-point check-in date of Oct 12, and write it all in the doc.

steps.title: Visit or study the coffee shop
steps.description: Spend time at the coffee shop (or its website and social pages) and note its menu, prices, atmosphere, customers, and current marketing. Done when you have a page of observations in the doc.

steps.title: Research competitors and local market
steps.description: Look at 3 nearby competing cafes and note their pricing, social media activity, and promotions. Add a short comparison table for your assigned section.

steps.title: Draft your first assigned section
steps.description: Write a rough draft of your first assigned section (e.g., situation analysis or target audience) in the shared doc, around 300-400 words. Rough is fine; done when it is on the page.

steps.title: Draft your second assigned section
steps.description: Write the strategies/channels or budget part you own, with specific tactics like Instagram campaigns, loyalty cards, or student discounts. Done when each tactic has a short explanation and rough cost.

steps.title: Mid-point team check-in
steps.description: Meet for 45 minutes to read each other's drafts, flag gaps or overlaps, and agree on the overall goals and key message. Write a list of revisions per person in the doc.

steps.title: Revise your sections
steps.description: Work through the revision list for your sections, tightening arguments and adding data or examples. Done when every comment on your part is resolved.

steps.title: Build timeline and metrics
steps.description: Together or split, write the campaign timeline and success metrics (e.g., follower growth, foot traffic, coupon redemptions). Done when both appear in the doc with clear dates and numbers.

steps.title: Create visuals and format the document
steps.description: Make 2-3 charts, tables, or mock social posts and apply consistent formatting, headings, and a title page. Done when the doc looks like a single cohesive piece.

steps.title: Write executive summary and conclusion
steps.description: Write a half-page executive summary and a short conclusion drawing from the finished sections. Done when both read consistently with the rest of the plan.

steps.title: Final team review meeting
steps.description: Meet for 60 minutes to read the entire plan aloud or skim it together, fix inconsistencies, and check against the assignment rubric. Done when everyone approves.

steps.title: Proofread and submit

plan.taskTitle: Finish reading Sapiens

steps.title: Put Sapiens on your pillow and set a bookmark
steps.description: Find your copy (or open the ebook), note the page or chapter you stopped at, and place the book where you'll see it tonight. Done when the book is open to your spot and a pen or sticky note sits next to it.

steps.title: Read for one 25-minute sprint and jot a 'wow' fact
steps.description: Set a 25-minute timer and read from where you left off without checking your phone. When it ends, write one surprising fact or idea on a sticky note as your souvenir.

steps.title: Read a 40-minute session with a challenge
steps.description: Set a 40-minute timer and try to beat your page count from last session. Mark one passage you disagree with using a pencil or highlight.

steps.title: Listen or skim: switch the format for 30 minutes
steps.description: Spend 30 minutes with the audiobook at 1.25x speed, or read while walking around. Done when you've covered another stretch of chapters in a different setting.

steps.title: Read a 45-minute session at a new spot
steps.description: Take the book to a cafe, library, or park bench and read for 45 minutes with a timer. Reward yourself with a snack once the timer rings.

steps.title: Do a 10-minute voice-memo recap
steps.description: Record yourself explaining the main argument of the chapters you've read since starting, as if telling a friend. Done when you have one short voice memo saved.

steps.title: Read a 40-minute session before bed
steps.description: Set a 40-minute timer and read in bed or on the couch with your phone in another room. Stop at a chapter end and bookmark it.

steps.title: Read a 45-minute session with a pencil
steps.description: Read for 45 minutes while underlining or noting one question per chapter in the margins. Done when you have at least two questions marked.

steps.title: Read a 45-minute push through the next chunk
steps.description: Set a timer for 45 minutes and read as many pages as you can. Count the pages remaining afterward and write the number on your sticky note.

steps.title: Read the final chapters in one last 40-minute stretch
steps.description: Set a 40-minute timer and read the remaining chapters through to the afterword. Done when you reach the last page.

steps.title: Write a 5-minute finish-line review

plan.taskTitle: Write a 3-page essay comparing Plato and Aristotle on justice
plan.analysis: With only about a day left, the plan compresses into a few short, low-pressure sessions tonight and tomorrow morning, starting with a tiny setup step and ending with a buffer for proofreading.

steps.title: Open a doc and paste in the prompt
steps.description: Just open a new doc named 'Plato vs Aristotle – Justice' and paste in the assignment prompt. That's it; you can close it afterward if you want.

steps.title: Gather your notes on Plato
steps.description: Just skim the Republic reading (Book I-IV, where Plato defines justice as each part of the soul and city doing its own work) and copy 3 quotes or ideas into your doc. Done when you have 3 bullets under a 'Plato' heading.

steps.title: Gather your notes on Aristotle
steps.description: Just skim Nicomachean Ethics Book V (justice as fairness, distributive vs. corrective justice) and copy 3 quotes or ideas under an 'Aristotle' heading. Done when you have 3 bullets.

steps.title: Write a rough 5-line skeleton
steps.description: Just type five messy lines: your main claim about how they differ, Plato's view, Aristotle's view, one key contrast, and one similarity. Nothing needs to be polished, and it's fine if it's wrong.

steps.title: Write the messy first draft, first half
steps.description: Just write the intro and the Plato section (about 1.5 pages) using your bullets. Let it be ugly; done when those two sections have words in them.

steps.title: Write the messy first draft, second half
steps.description: Just write the Aristotle section, the comparison, and a short conclusion to reach about 3 pages. Done when the draft reaches the end, however rough.

steps.title: Read it aloud and tidy up
steps.description: Just read the essay once, fix clunky sentences, check the page count, and add your citations. Then submit it, and you're finished.

plan.taskTitle: Finish 20 hypothesis testing problems in R
plan.analysis: Start by setting up the R script, then work through the 20 problems in four short batches spread from Thursday to Monday, leaving Tuesday as a buffer for checking and submitting.

steps.title: Set up your R script
steps.description: Open RStudio, create a new script named 'stats_hypothesis_hw.R', and paste in all 20 problems as comments. Done when the file is saved and loads the libraries you'll need.

steps.title: Review the hypothesis test functions
steps.description: Skim your lecture notes or textbook examples for t.test(), prop.test(), and chisq.test(), and write a 3-line cheat sheet at the top of your script showing the syntax of each. Done when you can see which function fits each problem type.

steps.title: Solve problems 1-5
steps.description: Write the R code for problems 1-5, state the null and alternative hypotheses in comments, and write one sentence on each conclusion. Done when all five run without errors and have written conclusions.

steps.title: Solve problems 6-10
steps.description: Code problems 6-10 the same way, with hypotheses, output, and a one-sentence conclusion for each. Mark any you're unsure about with a TODO comment.

steps.title: Solve problems 11-15
steps.description: Work through problems 11-15 with hypotheses, code, and conclusions. Done when every problem has output and a written interpretation using the p-value and significance level.

steps.title: Solve problems 16-20
steps.description: Finish problems 16-20 with hypotheses, code, and conclusions. Done when all 20 problems have code and an answer.

steps.title: Review, rerun, and submit
steps.description: Clear your environment and rerun the whole script top to bottom to confirm it works, resolve any TODO comments, and check that your conclusions match the p-values. Then export or format as required and submit before 11:59pm.

plan.taskTitle: Build a daily morning vitamin habit
